opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly my view has shifted quite a bit over the last few years.

When I first joined a big company, the appeal was obvious: you get resources you could never get in academia. You get compute, you get hardware, you get access to brilliant colleagues across many disciplines, and for robotics in particular, that matters a lot. Robots are expensive, they break, and you need a team of people just to keep a fleet running so you can collect data. A big company can absorb that cost in a way a university lab usually can't.

What's changed is that, as AI has become this intensely competitive race, the nature of the work inside a big company has changed too. In the earlier days, there was much more room for exploratory, curiosity-driven research. You could spend a year on an idea that might not work, and that was fine, because the goal was to push the frontier and publish. Now there's a much stronger sense of urgency. Everyone can see that foundation models are transforming the field, and the question is no longer just "is this interesting?" but "does this move us toward a product, toward a capability that matters, faster than everyone else?"

That has good and bad sides. The good side is focus. When a company decides something is a priority, it can concentrate an enormous amount of talent and compute on it, and you can make progress at a speed that's almost impossible elsewhere. Some of the most exciting work in robotics recently, connecting large vision-language models to robot control, really benefited from that kind of scale.

The harder side is that individual researchers have less freedom to wander. Projects become bigger, teams become larger, and your personal contribution can feel like a smaller piece of a very big machine. There's also more pressure, more secrecy, and less publishing than before, because what used to be research is now a competitive advantage.

So my view today is more nuanced. I still think big companies are among the best places to work on frontier AI, especially embodied AI, because the resource requirements keep growing. But I also think people should be very clear-eyed about what they want. If you want to be part of building something at massive scale, a big company is incredible. If you want to own a bold, contrarian idea end to end, the startup world, which has exploded in robotics recently, may be a better fit. I think that tension is something a lot of people in our field are thinking about right now, myself included.

r001.rationale: The response says big companies provide resources, including compute, that university labs usually lack. It does not identify that need as a reason university professors found companies or take part-time roles at large companies.

r002.rationale: The response describes companies concentrating talent and compute when work becomes a priority, but does not characterize this as a rare opportunity or say that people share a common goal.

fable-5.1.text:
It's changed a lot, honestly. Back when I first joined Google, I had the mindset that I'd be there forever. Big companies had the data, the compute, the talent, and if you wanted to work on frontier problems in AI, that's where you had to be. There was a kind of comfort in that. You could spend three or four years on one research direction, publish papers, and nobody was really breathing down your neck.

What's shifted is that the pace of the field has made the big-company tradeoffs much more visible to me. On one side, the resources are still unmatched. You cannot train certain models anywhere else, and that's not a small thing. But on the other side, I started to feel the gap between what I could see was possible and what I could actually ship. Every decision gets filtered through many layers, and when the whole field is moving in months instead of years, those layers start to feel expensive.

I also think the identity of a big-company researcher has changed. It used to be that you were a scientist who happened to work in industry. Now the incentives are much more product-driven, because every lab understands that models alone don't win. Distribution and products win. That's not necessarily bad, but it means the question you're asking yourself every day is different. It's less "what is true?" and more "what will matter to users six months from now?"

So the way I'd put it is this: I used to think of a big company as the destination. Now I see it more as one phase. It's a wonderful place to learn how things work at scale, to see how a large organization actually turns research into something millions of people use. But the competitiveness of AI has convinced me that the most important thing is to be in a position where you can move at the speed of your own convictions. For some people that's still inside a big company. For me, I found that I wanted a smaller surface area between an idea and the world.

r001.rationale: The response says large companies offer unmatched compute, but does not identify university professors founding companies or taking part-time roles at large companies because they need more computational resources.

r002.rationale: It describes large-company resources and tradeoffs, but does not characterize the opportunity through the combined conditions of computational resources, leadership prioritization, and a shared goal.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve come to appreciate both the advantages and the constraints more. At a big company, you have resources, infrastructure, and people with very deep expertise. As AI becomes more competitive, those things can matter a lot. You can pursue work that would be difficult for a small team to support.

But resources don’t automatically translate into progress. You still need to make decisions quickly, test ideas, and give people room to take risks. If coordination becomes too expensive, the advantage of being big can get lost.

So I’m less focused on company size itself. I’m more focused on whether a team can combine that support with the freedom and urgency to do good work.

r001.rationale: The response says large companies have resources and infrastructure, but does not identify computational-resource needs as a reason university professors found companies or take part-time roles.

r002.rationale: It describes large-company resources and expertise as advantages, but does not characterize the opportunity as rare or mention leadership prioritization and a shared goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become more aware of both the advantages and the constraints. At a big company, you have the resources to pursue ambitious ideas—compute, infrastructure, and people with deep expertise. As AI becomes more competitive, those advantages matter a lot.

But resources don’t automatically translate into progress. You also need to make decisions quickly, run experiments, and change direction when something isn’t working. A large organization can make that harder if every decision requires alignment across many teams.

So I’ve come to care less about company size by itself and more about how the team operates. Can a small group take ownership? Can researchers get feedback quickly? Can a promising idea actually reach users? To me, the attractive combination is the resources of a big company with the focus and speed of a small team.

r001.rationale: The response says large companies offer compute and other resources, but does not connect that need to university professors founding companies or taking part-time roles.

r002.rationale: It describes advantages of large-company resources, but does not characterize the arrangement as a rare opportunity or state that it depends on leadership prioritization and a shared goal.
